question: Can backpropagation-free zeroth-order optimization contribute stability, not just memory savings, in rehearsal-free class-incremental learning, and can a zeroth-order shared adapter plus first-order classifier preserve plasticity at low memory cost?

key_findings.claim: ZO-FC splits optimization by function: SPSA/ZO-SGD updates one shared rank-5 adapter in the first five frozen ViT blocks, while ordinary SGD updates a cosine classifier during the early half of each task's training.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4.2 motivates the split from failed direct substitutions. The experimental protocol fixes epsilon=0.001, Q=4, adapter and classifier learning rates 0.01, and a ViT-B/16 pretrained on ImageNet-21K. Algorithm 1 performs a classifier backward pass followed by Q two-sided Rademacher perturbations of the adapter.

key_findings.claim: Naively replacing first-order updates by low-query SPSA is a strong negative result: most learnable-classifier methods lose large amounts of accuracy, and gradient-sensitive prompt/orthogonality methods can collapse below random guessing.
key_findings.evidence: L2P, CODA-Prompt, and InfLoRA fail to converge under the common ZO budget; Table 2 reports CIFAR100 average accuracies of 15.05, 3.53, and 2.78, respectively, and similarly low ImageNet-R values. Extending prompt training to 100/200 epochs still leaves L2P at 26.43/11.83 and CODA-Prompt at 10.12/6.47 average accuracy on CIFAR100/ImageNet-R.

anchors.section: Supplement G, Table 8 extended prompt training

key_findings.claim: The component-swap ablation supports the adapter/classifier placement decision more directly than the flatness plots: reversing the optimizers causes catastrophic degradation.
key_findings.evidence: Table 6 compares ZO-FC with an FO adapter plus ZO classifier. On CIFAR100 the reverse placement drops average/last accuracy from 88.39/83.34 to 62.45/53.22 and raises forgetting from 5.26 to 25.65; on ImageNet-R it drops 72.01/66.63 to 23.35/11.72 and raises forgetting from 4.40 to 18.07.

key_findings.claim: On the single fixed Inc-5 stream, ZO-FC is competitive with several first-order PEFT baselines and has low forgetting, but it does not match the strongest first-order accuracy on all datasets.
key_findings.evidence: Table 2 gives ZO-FC average/last/forgetting of 88.39/83.34/5.26 on CIFAR100, 72.01/66.63/4.40 on ImageNet-R, and 77.17/71.05/4.19 on DomainNet. EASE is 91.13/85.45 on CIFAR100 and 78.78/71.93 on ImageNet-R; InfLoRA reaches 79.70/74.05 on DomainNet. Thus the strongest accuracy gaps are 2.74, 6.77, and 2.53 average-accuracy points, respectively.

key_findings.claim: The Inc-10 results repeat the stability pattern but also show that low forgetting is not equivalent to best overall accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: ZO-FC has the lowest displayed forgetting, 3.42 on CIFAR100 and 3.64 on ImageNet-R, with average accuracies 91.13 and 75.80. Multiple FO methods are above it in average accuracy: APER reaches 92.15 on CIFAR100, while EASE and InfLoRA reach 80.64 and 79.54 on ImageNet-R.

key_findings.claim: The theoretical forgetting expansion omits a generally nonzero first-order term, so the claimed direct curvature bound does not hold without an unstated old-loss stationarity assumption.
key_findings.evidence: For F_t=L_old(theta_t+Delta theta)-L_old(theta_t), Taylor expansion should contain grad L_old(theta_t)^T Delta theta before the quadratic term. Equation (3) drops it, although rehearsal-free training at the end of task t does not ensure stationarity of the cumulative old-task loss. Equation (4) also drops the cubic remainder when asserting an upper bound. Therefore the displayed chain from lower largest Hessian eigenvalue to lower forgetting is not established for the actual task sequence.

key_findings.claim: Even if zeroth-order smoothing lowers Hessian trace, the paper's implication that it lowers the largest Hessian eigenvalue is invalid in general.
key_findings.evidence: Equation (6) introduces a trace-Hessian term, while Eq. (7) changes the quantity to lambda_max(H_t). Trace and maximum eigenvalue need not move together; one can reduce the trace by changing other or negative-curvature directions while increasing the top eigenvalue. No PSD, spectral-shape, or trace-to-maximum condition is supplied.

key_findings.claim: The broad statement that ZO inherently minimizes curvature at convergence overextends both the Taylor expansion and the cited flat-minima theorem.
key_findings.evidence: The main text assumes only twice differentiability yet writes an O(epsilon^4) symmetric-smoothing remainder, which generally needs stronger fourth-order control. It then states that a stationary point of the smoothed loss minimizes the original-loss Hessian trace. The supplement narrows the cited theorem to convex, three-times differentiable losses with bounded third derivatives and roughly d^4/epsilon^2 iterations near a global optimum. None of convexity, global convergence, or that iteration regime is established for nonconvex ViT adapters trained on changing tasks.

anchors.section: Supplement C, proof assumptions for flat-minimum theorem

key_findings.claim: The supplementary hybrid proof is internally inconsistent with the actual estimator and training schedule.
key_findings.evidence: Supplement D calls the Rademacher two-point SPSA estimate an unbiased gradient of a Gaussian-smoothed loss, but Algorithm 1 samples Rademacher directions; unlike Gaussian smoothing, the stated estimator is not generally an exact smoothed-gradient identity for a discrete Rademacher distribution. The proof also assumes a faster classifier time scale with psi tracking argmin_psi L, although both learning rates are 0.01 and the classifier is frozen halfway through while the adapter continues. The reduced-objective dynamics therefore do not describe the implemented finite schedule.

anchors.section: Supplement A-B, equal learning rates and Rademacher Algorithm 1
Supplement D, Gaussian smoothing and fast-slow dynamics claim

key_findings.claim: The SAM-style flatness result is correlational and its normalized proxy has important confounds.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 5 reports lower old-task perturbation-loss change for ZO-FC than FO, but no numerical table, uncertainty, direction/norm sensitivity, or matched endpoint-loss control is given. Equation (8) divides by the old-task loss, so different base losses alter the score, and the paper itself says late-task convergence of the curves is partly a proxy artifact. Standard augmentation independently lowers forgetting substantially.

key_findings.claim: Query count exposes a genuine plasticity-stability trade-off rather than monotonic improvement from a better gradient estimate.
key_findings.evidence: On CIFAR100, Q=1 to 64 raises average accuracy only from 87.90 to 88.79 while forgetting worsens from 4.61 to 6.08. On ImageNet-R, average accuracy rises from 65.31 to 73.98, but forgetting is nonmonotone and remains 4.91 at Q=64 versus 3.0 at Q=1. The standard Q=4 point is therefore a design trade-off, not an optimum established by theory.

key_findings.claim: The reported memory benefit comes with materially greater total compute and the final FLOP table undercounts the early hybrid loop by one full model forward.
key_findings.evidence: Table 9 reports 0.70 GB for ZO-FC versus 4.35 GB for FO adapter+classifier. Table 10 reports 59.36 seconds/epoch at Q=4 versus 24.54 for FO. ZO-FC also trains its adapter for 20/40 epochs while comparable FO baselines use 10/20. The supplement correctly describes early ZO-FC as 2Q perturbation forwards plus one FO and one evaluation forward, i.e. 2Q+2, but Table 11 uses approximately 2Q+1 and assigns Q=4 only nine forward costs, making it numerically identical to pure ZO. At Q=4 this misses one of ten actual forwards and the paper never combines the approximately doubled epoch budget with per-epoch cost.

anchors.section: Supplement A, asymmetric 20/40 versus 10/20 epoch budgets

key_findings.claim: The evaluation has no independent replication: all reported streams use one class/task order and one seed, so optimizer stochasticity, order sensitivity, and uncertainty are unknown.
key_findings.evidence: Section 5.1 fixes seed 1993 for every dataset and method. Tables 2-8 provide single values without standard deviations, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or additional task-order runs.

anchors.section: Section 5.1, fixed task order and seed

key_findings.claim: The official code is substantial but does not provide a unique paper-matching Inc-5 reproduction path.
key_findings.evidence: The README's two Inc-5 commands name absent files. The existing un-suffixed CIFAR100 and ImageNet-R Inc-5 configs use Q=1 and Q=32, respectively, whereas the paper states Q=4. Only the Inc-10 configs consistently use Q=4. The repository contains one seed, no result logs/checkpoints, manual paths for ImageNet-R/DomainNet, and no automated test suite, so exact table regeneration remains ambiguous.

anchors.section: Supplement A, stated Q=4 reproduction settings

method.core_idea: Exploit the noisy, activation-free-memory character of SPSA as an implicit stability mechanism for a shared continual-learning adapter while reserving precise backpropagation for the classifier that must quickly form new decision boundaries.
method.mechanism: For each batch, SGD first updates the classifier using one backward pass. For each of Q Rademacher directions, the adapter is evaluated at plus/minus epsilon perturbations; their finite-difference losses are averaged into an SPSA gradient, clipped, and applied with ZO-SGD. The pretrained ViT backbone stays frozen, so adapter updates need no stored activations and classifier backpropagation terminates at the final head. The paper interprets the perturbation estimator as descent on a smoothed loss that biases the representation toward flat regions, while the FO head supplies plasticity.
assumptions: The pretrained ImageNet-21K ViT-B/16 representation is already sufficiently plastic that only a small shared adapter and classifier need training.
Rehearsal-free sequential class batches and the fixed seed-1993 order are representative of deployment streams.
Four SPSA query directions at epsilon=0.001 and gradient clipping 1.0 give an adequate adapter update under the chosen epoch budget.
The classifier can be treated as a faster subsystem that approximately tracks its optimum, despite equal nominal learning rates and being frozen halfway through training.
Smoothing current-task empirical loss leads to flatter old-task loss and lower catastrophic forgetting.
The trace of the Hessian is a meaningful, parameterization-robust flatness quantity and tracks the largest eigenvalue relevant to forgetting.
The convex flat-minimum theorem cited in the supplement transfers qualitatively to nonconvex adapter tuning on a changing task sequence.
A SAM-style normalized perturbation score is a valid proxy for loss-landscape flatness across methods with different endpoint losses.
Peak allocated GPU memory on an A6000 predicts resource use on the on-device hardware that motivates the work.
Accuracy comparisons remain informative despite ZO-FC using twice as many epochs and multiple forward evaluations per batch.

techniques.role: Assigns memory-light noisy updates to representation adaptation and precise gradients to the classifier.
Estimates the shared adapter gradient from plus/minus function evaluations along Q random sign directions.
Concentrates continual adaptation in rank-5 parallel modules in the first five frozen ViT blocks.
Updates the classifier only during the early half of each task while the ZO adapter continues for the full budget.
Swaps FO and ZO between adapter and classifier to identify which component is sensitive to gradient precision.
Measures normalized old-task loss increase after a fixed-radius parameter perturbation.
Varies SPSA direction count to expose accuracy, forgetting, and computation trade-offs.
Reports peak GPU allocation, measured epoch time, and estimated forward/backward FLOPs for FO, ZO, and hybrid updates.

evaluations.setting: Rehearsal-free CIFAR100 Inc-5 with ImageNet-21K ViT-B/16 and a single seed/order.

evaluations.result: ZO-FC obtains 88.39/83.34/5.26. EASE is higher accuracy at 91.13/85.45/7.05; FO Adapter+Classifier is 88.41/83.64/9.58.
evaluations.baseline: SimpleCIL and eight FO PEFT CIL methods plus their direct ZO substitutions.

evaluations.metric: Final average accuracy, last-task accuracy, and forgetting, percent.
evaluations.result: ZO-FC obtains 72.01/66.63/4.40. EASE reaches 78.78/71.93/7.54, and FO Adapter+Classifier reaches 74.71/69.62/8.49.
evaluations.baseline: SimpleCIL, FO PEFT methods, and their ZO substitutions.

evaluations.metric: Final average accuracy, last-task accuracy, and forgetting, percent.
evaluations.result: ZO-FC obtains 77.17/71.05/4.19, below InfLoRA's 79.70/74.05 accuracy and CODA-Prompt's 78.84/73.29, but with lower reported forgetting.

evaluations.result: ZO-FC reports 91.13/86.93/3.42 and 75.80/70.10/3.64. It has the lowest forgetting but trails the best FO average accuracy by 1.02 and 4.84 points.
evaluations.baseline: SimpleCIL and eight FO PEFT baselines.

evaluations.setting: FO/ZO placement and classifier-family ablations on Inc-5.
evaluations.result: FO adapter plus ZO classifier collapses to 62.45/53.22/25.65 on CIFAR100 and 23.35/11.72/18.07 on ImageNet-R. ZO adapter plus prototype also has higher forgetting than cosine ZO-FC; a linear ZO-FC head is much weaker on ImageNet-R.

Removing augmentation slightly raises average accuracy but increases forgetting from 5.26 to 8.02 on CIFAR100 and 4.40 to 5.19 on ImageNet-R.
evaluations.baseline: ZO-FC with standard random crop/flip augmentation.

evaluations.setting: A6000, batch 48 memory and runtime accounting.
evaluations.metric: Peak allocated GPU memory and seconds per epoch.
evaluations.result: ZO-FC uses 0.70 GB versus 4.35 GB for FO Adapter+Classifier. At Q=4, it takes 59.36 seconds/epoch versus 24.54 for FO; the paper's per-batch FLOP table estimates 3x FO but omits one early-loop forward.
evaluations.baseline: FO-SGD and pure ZO-SGD at Q=1 and Q=4.

evaluations.setting: SAM-style old-task loss perturbations over the CIFAR100 and ImageNet-R streams.
evaluations.metric: Normalized loss change Phi at a fixed perturbation radius.
evaluations.result: ZO-FC curves are lower than FO curves in Figure 5 and converge late in the stream; no numeric summary or uncertainty is reported.

limitations: [Author-stated] ZO has slower convergence and lower plasticity; matching the strongest FO methods may require a large query count or more advanced estimators.
[Author-stated] The work does not demonstrate actual on-device training, parallel perturbation execution, or harder fine-grained streams.
[Reviewer-identified] The Taylor forgetting argument omits the old-loss gradient term and remainder; theta_t is not shown to be stationary for cumulative old-task loss.
[Reviewer-identified] Hessian trace does not imply a smaller largest eigenvalue, so the central trace-to-forgetting causal chain has a missing condition.
[Reviewer-identified] The cited ZO flat-minimum theorem is convex/global and does not establish the claimed behavior for nonconvex ViT adapter optimization on sequential tasks.

[Reviewer-identified] Supplement D conflates Rademacher SPSA with an unbiased Gaussian-smoothed gradient and assumes a fast classifier time scale not implemented by the equal-learning-rate, half-frozen schedule.
[Reviewer-identified] All results use one seed and one task order; there are no confidence intervals, statistical tests, or order-sensitivity checks.

[Reviewer-identified] ZO-FC uses twice the adapter epochs of comparable FO baselines and Q=4 requires roughly ten early forward evaluations per batch, so accuracy is not compute- or wall-clock-matched.
[Reviewer-identified] The flatness score is loss-normalized, underspecified with respect to perturbation direction/norm in the main text, and reported only as a curve.
[Reviewer-identified] Standard augmentation materially lowers forgetting, confounding attribution of stability solely to ZO smoothing.
[Reviewer-identified] Peak CUDA allocated memory on one A6000 excludes an actual edge-device demonstration and may differ from reserved/device-total memory.
[Reviewer-identified] The official repository's missing README configs and conflicting Inc-5 Q values prevent a unique exact reproduction of Tables 2 and 4.
failure_modes: Gradient-sensitive prompt routing, contrastive penalties, and orthogonality constraints can fail to converge under low-query SPSA.
Applying ZO to the classifier produces poor decision boundaries and catastrophic accuracy loss even when the adapter is first-order optimized.
Very low forgetting can be vacuous when a method never learns new tasks; several collapsed direct-ZO baselines illustrate this metric pathology.
Increasing Q can improve ImageNet-R accuracy while worsening forgetting and multiplying compute, so no single query budget dominates.
If the pretrained representation is weak or the stream requires substantial feature change, a rank-5 shared adapter with noisy updates may lack plasticity.
Without replay, smoothing current-task loss need not preserve old-task loss when the two objectives have conflicting gradients or curvature bases.
The classifier-fast/adapter-slow interpretation fails when the classifier has not equilibrated before it is frozen.
Rademacher perturbations with a fixed global epsilon can be poorly scaled across heterogeneous adapter tensors.
The memory advantage can be outweighed by approximately fivefold total wall time or sixfold total FLOPs after accounting for Q=4 and doubled epochs.
Deployment may fail when parallel perturbation evaluations are unavailable or when device latency/energy, rather than peak memory, is the binding constraint.
reusable_insights: Optimizer precision can be allocated by module role: representation modules may tolerate noisy low-memory updates while classifier heads need precise gradients.
A component-swap ablation is more causally informative than comparing only complete hybrid methods.
Continual-learning reports should pair forgetting with accuracy/plasticity because a non-learning model can appear perfectly stable.
Query count is a three-way control over estimator variance, plasticity, and resource cost, not merely a quality knob.
Memory, runtime, FLOPs, and total epoch budget should all be reported; per-step memory savings alone can hide a large computation transfer.
Flatness arguments must track the same loss whose forgetting is measured and must distinguish trace, top eigenvalue, and perturbation-based sharpness.
open_questions: Does ZO-FC retain its ranking across task orders, seeds, harder fine-grained datasets, and weaker pretrained backbones?
Can a valid nonconvex sequential theorem relate Rademacher-smoothed current-task updates to old-task loss without assuming old-loss stationarity?
Which curvature statistic, if any, mediates the empirical effect: trace, largest eigenvalue, representation drift, or gradient interference?
Can dimension-aware/layerwise perturbation radii or variance-reduced ZO estimators recover plasticity at much lower Q?
How does ZO-FC compare at matched total energy, wall time, and FLOPs with C-Flat++, InfLoRA, replay, and ordinary FO adapters?
Does the classifier still require FO updates when prototypes, calibrated nearest-centroid heads, or analytic ridge heads are used?
Can an actual phone/edge accelerator run the perturbations in parallel while preserving the claimed 0.70 GB footprint?
Which exact public configuration generated the Inc-5 Q=4 tables, and can immutable logs/checkpoints resolve the current repository ambiguity?

competitive_landscape.title: AlterSGD: Finding Flat Minima for Continual Learning by Alternative Training
competitive_landscape.difference: AlterSGD already treats optimizer-induced flatness as a mechanism for reducing continual-learning forgetting. ZO-FC contributes a backprop-free adapter update and memory focus, not the original flat-minima-to-stability connection.

competitive_landscape.title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting in Incremental Few-Shot Learning by Finding Flat Minima
competitive_landscape.difference: This earlier work explicitly searches for flat base-task minima and restricts later fine-tuning to that region. Its setting is incremental few-shot learning; ZO-FC instead uses a shared pretrained-model adapter and claims intrinsic SPSA smoothing.

competitive_landscape.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models with Just Forward Passes
competitive_landscape.difference: MeZO establishes inference-like-memory ZO fine-tuning and compatibility with PEFT. ZO-FC transfers that resource idea to rehearsal-free vision CIL and adds an FO head, but the basic memory mechanism and two-sided in-place estimator are prior.

competitive_landscape.title: Revisiting Zeroth-Order Optimization for Memory-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning: A Benchmark
competitive_landscape.difference: This benchmark evaluates many ZO estimators, PEFT schemes, blockwise updates, sparsity, and hybrid training. ZO-FC is narrower but adds continual stability and the specific adapter/FO-classifier placement; it does not compare against this broader estimator set.

competitive_landscape.title: InfLoRA: Interference-Free Low-Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: InfLoRA explicitly projects low-rank updates into interference-free task subspaces to balance stability and plasticity. It attains higher DomainNet accuracy in the target's table but uses FO/backprop memory; ZO-FC trades precision and speed for lower activation memory.

competitive_landscape.title: Make Continual Learning Stronger via C-Flat
competitive_landscape.difference: C-Flat already makes zeroth- and first-order sharpness/flatness optimization plug-and-play across continual-learning categories. ZO-FC's distinction is using SPSA as the parameter optimizer for a PEFT adapter to eliminate backpropagation memory, rather than first introducing flatness-based CL optimization.

competitive_landscape.title: Zeroth-Order Optimization Finds Flat Minima
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper proves the convex smooth small-Hessian-trace selection result invoked almost verbatim in ZO-FC's supplement. ZO-FC's novelty is the CL application and hybrid module design; its nonconvex sequential use lies outside the antecedent theorem's guarantees.

competitive_landscape.title: C-Flat++: Towards a More Efficient and Powerful Framework for Continual Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: C-Flat++ reduces the update overhead of flatness-aware continual learning through selective promotion and reports broad CL comparisons. ZO-FC offers lower activation memory but substantially higher forward-query compute and does not benchmark directly against C-Flat++.

competitive_landscape.title: A Faster Path to Continual Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: C-Flat Turbo skips direction-invariant flatness gradients and schedules later-task updates to improve accuracy at lower overhead. It is a stronger compute-oriented comparison point than the target's proposed future parallelization, though it does not deliver the same backprop-free memory profile.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a novel use of zeroth-order optimization to address the plasticity-stability-efficiency trilemma in continual learning, a holistic audit showing why direct ZO substitutions fail, and ZO-FC as a memory-light hybrid that obtains flatter representations, lower forgetting, and accuracy comparable to FO PEFT methods.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Sections 3-4 connect smoothing to flatness and introduce the ZO-adapter/FO-classifier split; Tables 2-7 measure direct substitutions, main accuracy/forgetting, component placement, query count, and augmentation; Tables 9-11 report memory and compute.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The clearest novel contribution is the specific backprop-free SPSA shared-adapter plus FO cosine-classifier decomposition and its unusually broad failed-substitution/component-swap evidence in pretrained rehearsal-free CIL. ZO memory-efficient PEFT, hybrid ZO training, flat-minimum CL, and the exact convex ZO-flatness theorem are all prior. C-Flat already brings zeroth-order sharpness ideas to CL. The paper's mechanistic claim is substantially weaker than its engineering result because the forgetting Taylor series omits a term, trace is conflated with lambda_max, Rademacher and Gaussian smoothing are conflated, and the fast-slow dynamics do not match training.

The official v3 URL reproduced the indexed 16-page PDF hash exactly, and the indexed text has usable extraction on all 16 pages. Every main page, reference, algorithm, supplementary proof, table, ablation, memory/runtime derivation, and task-accuracy figure was read. The official code repository https://github.com/uncc-efficient-ai/ZOFC was audited at immutable HEAD 269102a72f3f58b1251255ed917ca6f2b327429d (2026-03-16): it contains extensive baseline/config code, but README Inc-5 filenames are absent, available Inc-5 Q values conflict with the paper, only seed 1993 is configured, datasets require manual paths, and no result artifacts or automated tests resolve the ambiguity. Confidence is medium for the reported single-stream table values and high for the component-swap negative; it is low for the claimed flatness-to-forgetting causal proof and for generalization to real on-device deployment.
